case.label: D
case.text: DynamoDB is fully managed and a skeptic could say an order system can be modeled with one table per entity. The stem rules it out: many relationships, joins in monthly reports and existing PostgreSQL SQL skills all point to a relational engine, and option D itself says one separate table for each entity, which gives no joins. Cue note: option C says 'as the only data store' and option A says 'one folder for each entity', so the two weak distractors are marked by their own wording; option B is the only one that names PostgreSQL.

answers.flag: Option E says only 'copy the data', so a careful candidate could read it as a one-time full load that does not fit the short cutover window; the stem never says ongoing replication, and D plus E is still the only workable pair.

case.label: A
case.text: Babelfish for Aurora PostgreSQL promises to run existing code on the new cluster without changes, and a candidate who half remembers it as a compatibility layer could pick it for hundreds of stored procedures with least overhead. It is a layer for SQL Server applications (T-SQL), not for Oracle PL/SQL, so it does not apply. Option B (an Aurora read replica of an Oracle database) is not possible either, because read replicas exist only between Aurora or RDS engines of the same family.

case.label: C
case.text: Removing (detaching) the secondary cluster makes it a standalone writable cluster in us-west-2 and is a long-standing way to recover from a Regional outage; it also accepts the loss of unreplicated writes. It loses only because the stem says the applications must keep the global writer endpoint and not change connection settings, and because it takes the cluster out of the global database. Option D (switchover) needs a healthy primary and the stem says the primary is unavailable. A reader who knows the older name 'managed planned failover' might hesitate over the phrase 'managed failover' in option A, but the outage still excludes the planned path.

case.label: B
case.text: A managed failover also moves the primary role to us-west-2 and keeps the global writer endpoint, so under time pressure it looks like the same result. The option itself says 'without waiting for the clusters to synchronize', which accepts data loss and contradicts the stated no-data-loss requirement, so it loses. The phrase is a strong cue; a candidate who only reads 'managed failover' vs 'switchover' as names would still need the stem's 'both Regions healthy' and 'no data loss' to decide, and both are given.

answers.flag: The stem gives no latency or scaling-speed number, so a careful candidate could defend Aurora Serverless v2 (option C) as fully managed, durable and load-scaling; the key rests on 'one item by key, no joins, sudden peaks of millions of requests' and on option B not naming a capacity mode.

case.label: C
case.text: Aurora Serverless v2 is durable, scales DB instance capacity with load, and needs no instance sizing, so it satisfies durability and elastic scaling. Against it: it still has a cluster, a capacity range to choose, and a single writer whose connection and write limits can be hit by sudden peaks of millions of requests, so it carries more operational work than a key-value table that needs no joins. Option D fails on durability (the stem says this is the only copy), and option A needs instance sizing and replicas.
